name: Transaction Cost
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: What You Pay to Play: Understanding Transaction Cost
lesson.summary: Transaction cost is the fee a user pays, denominated in gas, to have a transaction included in a block, and because block space is a hard-capped resource, that fee can spike sharply whenever demand for it outpaces supply.
lesson.body:
Every transaction submitted to a blockchain has to be validated, propagated, and permanently recorded by every node that maintains the network's full history, and someone has to be compensated for using that shared, finite resource. Transaction cost is the fee a user pays to have their transaction included in a block, and it exists because block space is scarce: a block can only hold so many transactions, or on Ethereum, so much computational work, and when more people want to transact than there is room for, they effectively bid against each other for inclusion. This is the practical, everyday face of the gas and fee mechanisms covered earlier, where gas measures the computational work a transaction requires and the fee is the price paid per unit of that work, denominated in the network's native currency.

The connection to computational cost is direct but distinct. Computational cost, discussed earlier, describes the resources a network spends to reach consensus in the first place, largely a mining or validation expense borne by the people securing the network. Transaction cost is the price an individual user pays to get their specific transaction processed, and while the two are related, since miners or validators are ultimately compensated partly through transaction fees, they are not the same number. A network can have low transaction fees during a quiet period even while its underlying computational cost of securing the chain stays roughly constant, because fees respond to short-term demand for block space while computational cost responds to longer-term participation in mining or validating.

A concrete example makes the mechanics clear. On Ethereum, a simple transfer of the network's native currency requires a fixed amount of gas, but a transaction that interacts with a complex smart contract, say, one that swaps a token on a decentralized exchange, requires much more gas because it triggers more computation. During periods of high demand, such as a popular new token launch or a market crash triggering mass selling, many users compete for the same limited block space simultaneously, and the fee per unit of gas can spike sharply within minutes, sometimes making a simple transfer cost more in fees than the amount being transferred. This volatility is a direct, observable consequence of block space being a hard-capped resource rather than something that scales automatically with demand.

Because transaction cost is paid by the end user for every single interaction, it becomes a real design constraint on decentralized applications built on top of any given chain. A lending protocol or exchange that requires several separate transactions to complete one user action multiplies that user's total cost, which is why application designers work hard to batch operations, and why entire categories of blockchain, sometimes running as layer-two networks on top of a base chain, exist largely to process many transactions more cheaply before settling a summary back to the more expensive base layer. Transaction cost, in other words, is not just an annoyance, it actively shapes how applications get built, which is a theme that continues in the next section on operating expense.
